title: Supreme Court Orders Separate 'High Fat, High Sugar, High Salt' Warnings on Packaged Foods
excerpt: A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran directed the FSSAI to mandate a separate pictorial hexagon for each nutrient, judged on total sugars and saturated fat, and to report progress on draft regulations in ten weeks.
body:
• Packaged foods high in fat, sugar or salt must carry a separate hexagonal warning for each nutrient, with a standard pictogram and the words "HIGH FAT", "HIGH SUGAR" or "HIGH SALT", the Supreme Court directed on Thursday.
  • Warnings must be judged on total sugars and saturated fat — not added sugar and added fat — and the FSSAI must reformulate its thresholds rather than adopt the Dietary Guidelines for India 2024 values as they stand.
  • Each hexagon must occupy 4% to 5% of the pack's principal display panel, with a font size prominent enough to read under normal conditions of purchase.
  • The court listed the matter after ten weeks for the FSSAI to report progress on draft regulations, and said the regulator's proposed timeline must be strictly adhered to.

The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Union Government and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to implement front-of-package nutrition labelling on packaged foods, ruling that products high in fat, sugar or salt must carry separate pictorial warnings for each nutrient of concern. A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran delivered the judgment in a public interest litigation filed by the organisation 3S and Our Health Society, in which judgment had been reserved on September 28.

One hexagon per nutrient

The court directed that the FSSAI ensure each hexagon in the labelling carries a standardised pictorial representation of the nutrient of concern together with the corresponding words "HIGH FAT", "HIGH SUGAR" or "HIGH SALT". There must be a separate hexagon for each nutrient rather than a single combined hexagon covering several, Live Law reported. Each hexagon should represent 4% to 5% of the principal display panel of the package, in line with international practice, and the FSSAI must prescribe a font size that keeps the warning prominent.

Total sugar and saturated fat, not "added"

The bench directed that front-of-pack labelling treat total sugars and saturated fat, rather than added sugar and added fat, as the nutrients of concern alongside salt — aligning with the consensus the FSSAI itself had reached in a 2021 stakeholder consultation. The authority must revisit and reformulate the threshold level for each nutrient on evidence, and the values in Table 15.1 of the Dietary Guidelines for India 2024 "shall not be adopted as they stand," since they were calculated with reference to added sugar and added fat, Bar and Bench reported.

The court warned against thresholds at either extreme: set too low, almost every packaged product would carry a warning and consumers would be desensitised by label fatigue; set too high, most products would escape the label and leave consumers unknowingly exposed to harmful levels of saturated fat, sugar and salt.

Timeline and next steps

The FSSAI had told the court it would need about four months to issue and finalise draft regulations, followed by a transition period of 365 days. The bench found the proposed timeline for implementation reasonable but directed the regulator to take all necessary steps, including preemptive ones, to ensure it is strictly adhered to, to prevent misuse of the transition period, and warned that no further extension shall ordinarily be granted. The matter will be listed again after ten weeks, when the FSSAI must report progress on the draft regulations by affidavit.

The court also directed the Union Government to ensure existing regulations, including the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020, are implemented strictly, and to build practical nutritional literacy among schoolchildren through curriculum changes, interactive workshops and co-curricular activities.

What shoppers will see

Once the regulations are notified and the transition period runs, a packet of biscuits or chips that crosses a threshold will carry up to three red hexagons on its front — one each for high fat, high sugar and high salt — instead of a single combined symbol. For now, nothing on shelves changes: the FSSAI's draft regulations are the next step, and the court will review progress in ten weeks.
